claims.text: Its three bonuses are real T-helper subsets: Th2 releases IL-5 to recruit eosinophils; Th17 releases IL-17, which drives G-CSF and steps up neutrophil production in the marrow; and direct contact is what licenses a B-cell to make antibodies properly.

claims.subject: Helper T-Cell
claims.label: In How to play
claims.text: It kills nothing. It licenses your other cells, and only after it has been primed.

claims.subject: Helper T-Cell
claims.label: In How to play
claims.text: Priming means an antigen has been presented, which happens the first time any of your cells engulfs or destroys a pathogen. With the B-Cell: +1 antibody per action. With the Killer T-Cell: +1 range. With the Eosinophil: +1 step. In the bloodstream: the Neutrophil returns in 2 turns.

claims.subject: NK Cell
claims.label: The name we use
claims.text: The app calls this piece the NK Cell, for the real-world nk.

claims.subject: NK Cell
claims.label: What it does
claims.text: The innate killer. It needs no antigen and no priming, so it attacks an infected cell at once, but it rolls a die, and hits on a 3 or more.

claims.subject: NK Cell
claims.label: Where it comes from
claims.text: The bloodstream, patrolling on its own. In the game it starts in the Bloodstream, moves two steps per Action Point, and reaches one step around it.

claims.subject: NK Cell
claims.label: What it is best against
claims.text: The same hidden targets as the Killer T-Cell, viruses and protozoa inside your own cells, earlier and less reliably. Its reach is one step; the Killer T-Cell reaches further and never misses.

claims.subject: NK Cell
claims.label: What happens without it
claims.text: People born without NK cells suffer repeated, severe herpesvirus infections: the viruses that hide inside cells early, before the T-cells are ready.

claims.subject: NK Cell
claims.label: Card fact
claims.text: NK cells kill cells that have stopped showing their identity papers. A virus that hides a cell's surface markers from T-cells makes that cell a target for NK cells instead.

claims.subject: NK Cell
claims.label: In How to play
claims.text: NK strike: attacks a hidden or infected cell within one step, on a die roll of 3 or more.

claims.subject: NK Cell
claims.label: In How to play
claims.text: Needs no antigen and no antibody.

claims.subject: Eosinophil
claims.label: The name we use
claims.text: The app calls this piece the Eosinophil, for the real-world eosinophil.

claims.subject: Eosinophil
claims.label: What it does
claims.text: The anti-parasite specialist. It strikes a coated worm or parasite for 2 damage, or degranulates for 3, enough to kill a worm outright, at the price of burning the organ it stands in and four turns spent.

claims.subject: Eosinophil
claims.label: Where it comes from
claims.text: Made in the marrow, circulating in small numbers and recruited to wherever a parasite is. In the game it starts in the Bloodstream and gains a step beside a primed Helper T-Cell. That is IL-5.

claims.subject: Eosinophil
claims.label: What it is best against
claims.text: Worms and large parasites, once antibodies have coated them. It cannot touch an uncoated one, and it is no use against bacteria or viruses.

claims.subject: Eosinophil
claims.label: What happens without it
claims.text: Without eosinophils the body loses its specialist weapon against worms, and some worm infections take longer to clear. Where they are over-active, the same granules turn on the body's own airways. That is asthma and allergy.

claims.subject: Eosinophil
claims.label: Card fact
claims.text: Eosinophil granules are indiscriminate poison. That is why parasitic infections cause chronic inflammation and scarring, and why degranulating should feel like a decision rather than a free hit.

claims.subject: Eosinophil
claims.label: In How to play
claims.text: Strike: 2 damage to a coated worm or parasite.

claims.subject: Eosinophil
claims.label: In How to play
claims.text: Degranulate, 2 AP: 3 damage, enough to kill a worm outright, but it burns the organ it stands in and the cell is spent for 4 turns.

claims.subject: The resident macrophages
claims.label: In How to play
claims.text: One lives in each organ. Patrol: 1 AP per step along its own organ branch.

claims.subject: The resident macrophages
claims.label: In How to play
claims.text: It may never leave that branch, and it must be out on the branch to meet anything: nothing can be engulfed in the organ box itself. Engulf, free once per turn: destroy one virus or coated bacterium on its space.

claims.subject: Cardiac macrophage
claims.label: The name we use
claims.text: The macrophage that lives in the Heart is called the Cardiac macrophage.

claims.subject: Alveolar macrophage
claims.label: The name we use
claims.text: The macrophage that lives in the Lungs is called the Alveolar macrophage.

claims.subject: Kupffer cell
claims.label: The name we use
claims.text: The macrophage that lives in the Liver is called the Kupffer cell.

claims.subject: Microglia
claims.label: The name we use
claims.text: The macrophage that lives in the Brain is called the Microglia.

claims.subject: Marrow macrophage
claims.label: The name we use
claims.text: The macrophage that lives in the Bone Marrow is called the Marrow macrophage.

claims.subject: Splenic macrophage
claims.label: The name we use
claims.text: The macrophage that lives in the Spleen is called the Splenic macrophage.

claims.subject: Renal macrophage
claims.label: The name we use
claims.text: The macrophage that lives in the Kidneys is called the Renal macrophage.

parts.title: Part 4 — The antigen classes
parts.blurb: The app groups pathogens into six classes by what an antibody actually binds to, and shows this description of each. Which disease we put in which class is a game decision and is not included; whether the description of the class is true is not.

claims.subject: Enveloped virus
claims.label: What it is
claims.text: Wrapped in a stolen piece of your own cell membrane, studded with spike proteins. Antibodies target the spikes.

claims.subject: Naked virus
claims.label: What it is
claims.text: No envelope. A bare protein shell. Tough, survives on surfaces, and antibodies must grip the capsid itself.

claims.subject: Extracellular bacterium
claims.label: What it is
claims.text: Lives outside your cells, often behind a slimy capsule. Antibodies opsonise it so phagocytes can grip it.

claims.subject: Intracellular bacterium
claims.label: What it is
claims.text: Hides INSIDE your cells, where antibodies struggle to follow. This is why TB is so hard to kill.

claims.subject: Toxin (antitoxin)
claims.label: What it is
claims.text: Not alive at all. Cannot be eaten. Antibodies (antitoxin) are the ONLY defence.

claims.subject: Eukaryotic parasite
claims.label: What it is
claims.text: Fungi, worms and protozoa. Complex cells like ours, so they are hard to target without harming yourself.

parts.title: Part 5 — The organs
parts.blurb: What the app says about how infection reaches each organ. The damage each organ takes before it is lost is a game number and is not included.

claims.subject: Heart
claims.label: How infection reaches it
claims.text: The heart itself can be infected. Staph on the valves (endocarditis), Lyme carditis, viral myocarditis. Germs only passing through the bloodstream do NOT infect it; only germs that target heart tissue do.

claims.subject: Lungs
claims.label: How infection reaches it
claims.text: Damaged lungs mean poor gas exchange. The whole body weakens.

claims.subject: Liver
claims.label: How infection reaches it
claims.text: The liver makes many defence proteins; damage it and antibody supply falls.

claims.subject: Bone Marrow
claims.label: How infection reaches it
claims.text: All immune cells are made in the marrow.

claims.subject: Brain
claims.label: How infection reaches it
claims.text: Immune privilege: the blood-brain barrier keeps immune cells out, so it is hard to defend and cannot take much damage.

claims.subject: Spleen
claims.label: How infection reaches it
claims.text: The spleen filters encapsulated bacteria from the blood. Without it, bacterial infection runs wild.

claims.subject: Kidneys
claims.label: How infection reaches it
claims.text: Damaged kidneys leak antibodies into the urine. A real cause of secondary immunodeficiency.

parts.title: Part 6 — Why each event happens
parts.blurb: Things that happen to the body during a game. Each carries a one-sentence reason, which is the app explaining pathophysiology in the smallest space it ever uses, and therefore where a compression error is most likely. What the event does in the game is not included.

claims.subject: Immunosuppression
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: Stress or malnutrition blunts the response.

claims.subject: Neutropenia
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: Neutrophil count crashes.

claims.subject: Lymphopenia
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: A virus is destroying lymphocytes.

claims.subject: Antibody shortage
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: Plasma cells can't keep up.

claims.subject: Fatigue
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: The whole body is exhausted: 1 fewer Action Point this turn only.

claims.subject: Co-infection
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: A second germ slips in while you're busy.

claims.subject: Acute-phase surge
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: Inflammation floods the tissue with defenders: +2 Action Points this turn only. (Acute-phase proteins and a burst of cells released from the marrow.)

claims.subject: Passive antibodies
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: A booster tops up your antibodies.

claims.subject: Fever
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: Raised temperature slows the invaders (at an energy cost).

claims.subject: Malaria relapse
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: A dormant hypnozoite of P. vivax woke up in your liver — months later, from nothing. This is why vivax malaria needs a second drug to clear the liver.

claims.subject: Dengue — antibody-dependent enhancement
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: Your dengue antibodies from last time do NOT neutralise this serotype — they HELP it into your cells. Your own immune memory is being used against you. This is why the second dengue infection is the dangerous one.

claims.subject: TB reactivation
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: Latent TB woke up while your defences were down. A quarter of the world carries TB silently.

claims.subject: Shingles
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: The chickenpox virus never left — it hid in your nerves for years and has re-emerged.

claims.subject: Post-influenza pneumonia
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: Flu stripped your airway lining and bacteria moved in. This is what killed most victims of the 1918 pandemic — not the flu itself.

claims.subject: Rheumatic fever
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: MOLECULAR MIMICRY: your anti-Strep antibodies cannot tell the difference between the bacterium and your own heart valve — so they are attacking your heart. A leading cause of heart disease in Indian children.

claims.subject: Cytokine storm
claims.label: The reason given
claims.text: Your immune response went into overdrive and the inflammation itself burned an organ. This is what killed young, healthy people in COVID and in 1918 — the response, not the germ.

parts.title: Part 7 — "Why it works this way"
parts.blurb: Fifteen passages that explain how immunity works in general, rather than describing one disease. These are the ones most likely to be quoted at a science fair or read aloud by a teacher, and they make the broadest claims in the app.

claims.subject: Why surviving the window is not the win
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: Real infections do not end when the exposure stops. They end when the last organism is cleared. A person is not well the moment they stop being infected; they are well when their body has finished the job. That is why surviving the window is not a win.

claims.subject: Why the Blood route is short
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: The Blood route is short because a needle, a transfusion or a deep wound puts an infection straight into the bloodstream, skipping the skin, the mucus and the stomach acid that stop almost everything else. Bloodborne infection is fast because it has cheated the barriers.

claims.subject: Why the lymphatic shortcuts join the routes they do
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: Mucosal surfaces share a common defensive system (MALT), and skin wounds drain to shared regional lymph nodes. A needle into a vein bypasses lymphatic drainage entirely, which is exactly why the Blood route has no shortcut.

claims.subject: Why the Brain is so hard to defend
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: The blood-brain barrier deliberately keeps immune cells out, to protect neurons that cannot be replaced. That protection is also a weakness: it is why brain infections are so hard to clear, and why the Brain has only 2 integrity instead of 3.

claims.subject: Why you start with no antibodies
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: You start with zero antibodies because the first adaptive response genuinely takes five to ten days: the one matching B-cell must be found among millions and then multiplied. The innate cells exist to buy exactly those days.

claims.subject: Why worms do not multiply inside you
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: Worms are large animals that burrow into tissue rather than travelling in the blood like a virus. And unlike bacteria they cannot multiply inside you: most human worms lay eggs that must leave the body and develop outside. A person's worm burden grows through repeated exposure, not internal breeding, which is why two per game is biologically honest as well as playable.

claims.subject: Why coating a toxin-maker stops its countdown
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: Coating a toxin-making bacterium stops its countdown completely: a coated bacterium never advances toward releasing its toxin. That is the game rewarding you for dealing with tetanus early, which is exactly the clinical advice.

claims.subject: Why coating is not killing
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: Coating is separated from killing on purpose. An antibody is a handle, not a weapon. This is opsonisation, and it is why the B-Cell and the Monocyte have to work as a pair.

claims.subject: Why the Helper must be primed first
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: A naive helper T-cell genuinely cannot help anyone until a dendritic cell presents it an antigen. The three bonuses are the real T-helper subsets: Th2 releases IL-5 to recruit eosinophils, Th17 releases IL-17 which drives G-CSF and steps up neutrophil production in the marrow, and helper contact is what licenses a B-cell to make antibodies properly.

claims.subject: Why the NK Cell rolls a die
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: The NK cell is innate: it needs no antibody, no antigen presentation and no priming, so it works from turn one. The die is the honest price of that speed. It is fast and always available, but less precise than a Killer T-Cell.

claims.subject: Why the Eosinophil burns the organ it stands in
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: Eosinophil granules are indiscriminate poison. Killing a parasite inside tissue damages that tissue, which is why parasitic infections cause chronic inflammation and scarring, and why degranulating should feel like a decision rather than a free hit.

claims.subject: Why a resident never leaves its organ
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: Tissue-resident macrophages, Kupffer cells in the liver, alveolar macrophages in the lungs, microglia in the brain, live permanently in one organ and never circulate. The 'never leaves' rule is what tissue-residency means.

claims.subject: Why malaria needs three different defences
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: This is the clearest example in medicine of why the same pathogen needs different defences at different moments. The RTS,S malaria vaccine targets the travelling sporozoite precisely because that brief window is when antibodies can act at all.

claims.subject: Why you must vaccinate on Normal and Hard
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: On the harder modes the game forces the real public-health lesson: waiting to catch a disease is a terrible strategy. A vaccine gives you the memory without the illness, and paying 5 Action Points before an outbreak is far cheaper than fighting it twice.

claims.subject: Why Pathogen X takes so long to answer
claims.label: The passage
claims.text: This is clonal selection, and the delay is the point: it is precisely why a genuinely new virus is so dangerous. Your body is not missing the tools; it is searching a library of a hundred million receptor shapes for the one that fits.

parts.title: Part 8 — General statements about how the body works
parts.blurb: Sentences from How to play that explain immunology in general rather than describing one disease, cell or pathogen. Rules text is filtered out aggressively, so this part is short by design: most of what How to play says about a particular cell or invader has already appeared under that subject in Parts 2 and 3.

claims.subject: How to play
claims.label: s1.p2
claims.text: Each of you commands one immune cell. Alone, every cell is nearly useless: the Monocyte cannot swallow a worm, the Killer T-Cell cannot touch a toxin, and the B-Cell's antibodies cannot reach anything hiding inside your own cells. Together, you can hold.

claims.subject: How to play
claims.label: s7.p1
claims.text: An antibody only fits its own antigen class. Making the wrong one is wasted work.

claims.subject: How to play
claims.label: s9.rare
claims.text: A few cards carry rarer events that fire at the end of a spread, such as a malaria relapse or shingles. The log names each one and says why.
